description: We’re taking on a health challenge with MedAR, an augmented reality interface for astronauts. It tracks your hand live and overlays step-by-step guidance for medical procedures, like showing exactly where to make an incision using a standard med kit. It also turns a daily strain score into an AR exercise game, so if a crew member hasn’t been active enough, they fly through virtual hoops to hit their target. We already have a working prototype with hand tracking, live vitals and the strain game.
summary:
MedAR is a browser-based health assistant that turns a helmet camera into a crew medical tool. It runs on a phone camera in our demo and needs nothing to install.

It answers the challenge of giving astronauts a visual tool to assess their health and act on it. A 40-second scan measures hand steadiness, balance and sway, and alertness (blink rate and eye closure) with no sensors to wear, then colour-codes each result as Nominal, Watch or Flag and logs it. Seven guided procedures, including CPR, a tourniquet and burn care, draw each step on the patient in the visor, with microgravity notes. A camera-tracked workout counts real squats and jumping jacks toward a daily strain target.

This matters because on deep-space missions a message between Mars and Earth can take up to 22 minutes one way, so crews must spot health changes and treat emergencies themselves. MedAR maps to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight and gives crews instructions for their hands, not just warnings.

Tracking runs on the device, so no video leaves it. Vitals and suit readings are simulated, and scan thresholds are unvalidated demo values pending clinician review.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

MedAR is a helmet-camera health assistant for astronauts on deep-space missions, where a message between Mars and Earth can take up to 22 minutes one way and crews must act as their own doctors. It does three things with one camera and no wearable sensors:

1. DETECT:

A 40-second scan of a crewmate measures hand steadiness (fingertip tremor from 21 tracked hand points, 10 s), balance and sway (side-to-side upper-body drift from 33 tracked body points, 10 s) and alertness (blink rate and time with eyes closed, 15 s). Each result is colour-coded Nominal, Watch or Flag and saved to a crew health log, so changes can be compared against each person's own baseline.

2. TREAT:

Seven guided procedures draw each step directly on the patient in the visor: laceration care and closure, radial pulse check, finger splint, minor burn care, CPR, tourniquet and deltoid injection. Every step gives a plain instruction, an on-body marker showing where to act, a timer where it matters, the kit to fetch, and when to escalate to the flight surgeon. Each procedure carries an "In space" note, for example bracing yourself for CPR, containing floating blood, and cooling a burn with soaked dressings because water will not run off.

3. TRAIN:

Body tracking counts real squats (by knee angle) and jumping jacks toward a daily strain target, turning the exercise that protects muscle and bone into a game.

BENEFITS

- A health check with nothing to wear or unpack.

- Guidance on what to do with your hands, not just a warning that something is wrong. - Works without a link to the ground.

- Tracking runs on the device, so no video leaves it.

- Each feature answers one of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight: radiation (running dose display), isolation and confinement (alertness check), distance from Earth (seven procedures that need no ground link), gravity fields (balance scan and workout) and hostile, closed environments (suit oxygen, CO2 and pressure in view).

INTENDED IMPACT

To help crews notice small health changes early and act on them confidently when help is minutes to hours away. The same approach could support remote clinics, field expeditions and disaster response.

BUILT WITH

A web app that runs in any modern browser with on-device hand, body and face tracking (MediaPipe-based), using a phone camera to stand in for a helmet camera. Vitals, suit readings and radiation dose are simulated.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It combines detection, treatment and training on a single camera, and draws guidance on the patient instead of in a manual. It is built around NASA's own hazard research, and the microgravity notes adapt standard first aid to conditions where fluids and bodies behave differently.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

NASA's five hazards; microgravity; privacy (on-device tracking); and honesty about limits. Scan thresholds are demonstration values and are not clinically validated, and the medical wording is standard first-aid guidance that still needs review by a clinician. Next steps are connecting real suit and wearable sensor feeds, charting each crew member's trend against their own baseline, validating thresholds and wording with flight surgeons, and prompting a daily scan.
